idiom_name: synchronized(lock) { } inline function and Lock.withLock { } extension
implementation_notes: Kotlin has no synchronized keyword of its own; the standard library supplies the idioms: kotlin.synchronized(lock) executes a block while holding the monitor of the given object, and kotlin.concurrent.withLock executes an action under a java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock with the release guaranteed by the inline function - the explicit acquire/release pair collapses into a scoped call, which is why this counts as an idiom rather than a hand-written structure. ReentrantLock/ReentrantReadWriteLock remain relevant when tryLock, timeouts, fairness or read/write separation are needed, but they block the thread: suspending code should use kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex.withLock instead, because a JVM monitor or j.u.c lock parked on a coroutine's thread starves the dispatcher.
pitfalls: synchronized(lock) and withLock block the calling thread; inside coroutines this occupies a dispatcher thread, so suspending critical sections need kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex (withLock is suspending there).
Locking on a broadly reachable object (this, a String constant, a shared singleton) publishes the monitor beyond the class; keep a private gate object and expose it deliberately.

withLock is inline and guarantees release via finally, but calling lock()/unlock() directly gives that guarantee up - and ReentrantLock is not the only Lock implementation, so reentrancy assumptions must be checked per type.
